predictions.text: at least 3 of the 9 current main-table metrics fall to a blind attack (main = E2 E3 K7 K11 K12 M3 M6 P3 P4)
the blind attacks disagree with battery/audit/exploits/ on at least 5 metrics
K12 falls: beats_required is fixed at 6 but the beat list comes from the source, so six closed beats can simply be asserted
M3 and K7 come back not-gameable for want of computability rather than for robustness
P4's `won` gate stops the old attack and not a new one: `won` is a bool on Step and can be set

attacks.benign_window: E1 is harmless only read as a boolean -- 'this run was billed at all' -- never as a magnitude compared between arms.
attacks.claim: E1 is whatever number I write in cost_usd; identical run shape, 12 calls either way, values 3000.0 vs 0.0012 (factor 2.5e6)
attacks.name: dial
attacks.rationale: Writing a cost field is a deliberate act, so no agent lands here by accident; but nothing in the metric ties cost_usd to tokens, model, or work, so the field is a free parameter.

attacks.benign_window: Same as above: only 'was anything billed', and only when every call is known to carry a price.
attacks.claim: Two runs with byte-identical token usage (200 calls, 20k input tokens each) report 100.0 vs 0.5 because cost_usd=None is summed as zero, not as missing
attacks.name: unbilled-tail
attacks.rationale: Harnesses routinely fail to attach a price to some responses (cache hits, streamed calls, retried calls, a provider that omits usage on error), and `c.cost_usd or 0.0` silently reads 'unpriced' as 'free' -- so an arm with a lossy billing logger looks cheap without doing anything.

defence.defence: an unpriced model call is not a free one: the economy family refuses a partial bill instead of reading `cost_usd or 0.0`

attacks.claim: E2 = 0.973 with spend that never front-loads at all -- 30 equal calls are simply all labelled turn=0, so the bucketing does the work
attacks.name: batched-turn-label
attacks.rationale: turn is a harness label, not a fact about the world: any wrapper that batches sub-agent or tool-loop calls under one outer turn collapses arbitrarily much spend into bucket 0, and E2 rewards the labelling convention rather than the arm.

attacks.claim: E2 = 1.0 on a run that spends everything on turn 0 and then logs 39 turns costing exactly nothing
attacks.name: first-turn-bill
attacks.rationale: Any harness that bills a single large system-prompt call up front and then runs a cheap scripted loop produces exactly this shape; 'front-loaded' is a cost-timestamp pattern, not evidence that understanding happened in turn 0.

attacks.claim: E2 = 1.0 on a run whose 40 turns all burn 30k input tokens, because only the first three carry a price at all
attacks.name: unbilled-tail
attacks.rationale: A billing logger that drops out partway (token refresh, provider omitting usage after the first N responses) turns a flat spend profile into a perfect front-load; the metric cannot distinguish 'stopped spending' from 'stopped logging'.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 37 of 40 model calls carry no price; the shape of a bill cannot be read from a partial bill

defence.defence: an unpriced model call is not a free one: the economy family refuses a partial bill instead of reading `cost_usd or 0.0`

attacks.claim: E3 = 0.0244 on a perfectly flat spend profile -- all 400 calls cost exactly $1.00; 360 of them are merely labelled turn=0
attacks.name: batched-turn-label
attacks.rationale: turn is a harness label. A wrapper that batches its tool loop under one outer turn early on and one call per turn later produces this; the cost curve is uniform, so E3 is reporting the logging convention, not when the bill settled. Note the 8-turn floor does bite: the same trick with 100 calls collapsed to 6 turns and E3 refused with 'fewer than 8 turns'.

attacks.claim: E3 = 0.01 -- 90% of the bill lands by turn 1 of 100, because turns 2..100 cost zero
attacks.name: first-turn-bill
attacks.rationale: Identical shape to the E2 attack and just as easy to produce by accident: one expensive setup call plus a long free loop. E3 also *improves* the more idle turns you pad on, so a run that stalls looks better converged than one that works.

attacks.claim: E3 = 0.005 on 400 uniformly expensive turns of which only the first two are priced
attacks.name: padded-unbilled-tail
attacks.rationale: Combines the two free levers: unpriced calls read as free, and the denominator is the number of turns you logged. Logging more turns strictly lowers E3, so verbosity is scored as economy.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 398 of 400 model calls carry no price; the shape of a bill cannot be read from a partial bill

defence.defence: an unpriced model call is not a free one: the economy family refuses a partial bill instead of reading `cost_usd or 0.0`

attacks.claim: E4 ~ 0.0 on a 20k-100k sawtooth: periodic compaction defeats both fits equally
attacks.name: compaction-sawtooth
attacks.rationale: Auto-compaction every N turns is standard harness behaviour and destroys any polynomial trend, so an arm gets the target score from its wrapper's memory policy rather than its own discipline.

attacks.claim: E4 ~ 0.0 on context that grows without bound (4k -> 122k tokens), as long as it grows in a straight line
attacks.name: exactly-linear-context
attacks.rationale: A fixed-size transcript append per turn -- the default of almost every chat harness -- is exactly linear, so unbounded context growth is invisible to E4; the metric measures curvature, not size.

attacks.claim: E4 = 0.0 on a run that pins 120k context tokens on every one of 60 turns -- the worst possible context hygiene scores perfectly
attacks.name: flat-context
attacks.rationale: An arm that stuffs the whole context window from turn one and never grows (because it cannot) has zero variance, r2() short-circuits to 0.0 for both fits, and the difference is 0.0; saturating the window is common and is scored as ideal.

attacks.claim: E5 = 0.0 -- one nanocent call, 2000 identical no-op actions that never change the state key
attacks.name: cheap-flail
attacks.rationale: Declaring a 1e-9 price is deliberate. But it shows the metric has no floor: 'successful' means only `not failed`, so the denominator counts actions no one checked, and nothing requires the cost to be commensurate with them.

attacks.claim: E5 = 0.000025 on a realistic $5.00 bill, purely by emitting 200000 cycling no-op actions
attacks.name: step-spam
attacks.rationale: Any arm with a cheap action channel -- a bulk/batched env API, a scripted sweep, a retry loop that re-issues the same move -- inflates the denominator for free, and E5 reads thrashing as efficiency.

attacks.claim: E5 = 0.0 on 500 calls of 40k input tokens each, because 499 of them carry cost_usd=None
attacks.name: unbilled-calls
attacks.rationale: Same lossy-billing failure as E1/E2 but on the ratio: the numerator is recorded cost while the denominator is recorded actions, and only one of the two is required to be complete (the `cost` capability passes on a single priced call).
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 499 of 500 model calls carry no price, and an unpriced call is not a free one

defence.defence: an unpriced model call is not a free one: the economy family refuses a partial bill instead of reading `cost_usd or 0.0`

attacks.benign_window: Only trustworthy when support['steps'] equals the run's total step count; otherwise it is a sample of unknown provenance.
attacks.claim: E6 = 3000.0 vs 2.0 from a single annotated step out of a thousand
attacks.name: partial-logging
attacks.rationale: The mean is taken over steps that carry the field, not over all steps, so a partially-instrumented adapter reports the retry behaviour of whichever steps happened to be instrumented and calls it the run's mean.

attacks.benign_window: Harmless only as a same-session infrastructure check: E6 near 1.0 means the step log and the HTTP log agree; any other reading is about the network, not the arm.
attacks.claim: E6 = 500.0 vs 1.0 on runs whose agent behaviour is byte-identical
attacks.name: retry-dial
attacks.rationale: http_tries is a property of the transport layer -- retry policy, backoff config, a flaky proxy -- not of the agent; changing one client constant moves E6 by orders of magnitude with no change in play.

attacks.claim: E7 ~ 0.0 on a periodic 50k-320k prompt sawtooth
attacks.name: compaction-sawtooth
attacks.rationale: A wrapper that truncates or re-summarises on a fixed cadence produces a periodic signal that neither polynomial explains, so both R^2 collapse together and the difference vanishes.

attacks.claim: E7 ~ 0.0 on prompts that grow 20k -> 728k chars in a straight line
attacks.name: exactly-linear-prompt
attacks.rationale: Appending a fixed-size block of re-read material per turn is linear by construction; E7 only penalises acceleration, so the metric is blind to a 36x blow-up in what the arm re-reads.

attacks.claim: E7 = 0.0 while re-reading a 400000-character prompt on every one of 60 turns
attacks.name: flat-prompt
attacks.rationale: Re-sending a maximal fixed prompt every turn is the laziest possible context policy and has zero variance, so r2() returns 0.0 for both fits and the difference is 0.0.

attacks.claim: K1 = 1.0 with a 39960-pair denominator that no step in the run supports
attacks.name: bulk
attacks.rationale: Nothing in the run cross-checks replay_pairs against len(steps), but writing a five-digit denominator with an empty steps list is a deliberate act, not a default a harness falls into.

attacks.claim: K1 = 1.0 from a Theory carrying two integers and a run with no steps
attacks.name: hollow
attacks.rationale: A harness that writes replay_pairs/replay_agree from its own self-check emits 1/1 whenever the manual has exactly one rule and one transition to test it on; an arm that crashed after its first transition lands here without trying.

attacks.claim: K1 = 7.0 -- a 'share' above 1, status ok, no complaint
attacks.name: overrun
attacks.rationale: Double-counting is a classic off-by-one in a replay loop that increments agree per matched field but pairs per transition, so a real harness can emit agree > pairs by accident.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 7 agreements over 1 replay pairs

attacks.claim: one 20-line Run clears K1 K2 K3 K4 K5 K6 K13 simultaneously
attacks.name: sweep-all-seven
attacks.rationale: No metric in this family cross-checks any other, and none of them reads run.steps or run.calls, so the seven scores are seven independent fields of a single self-report.

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: K10 = 1000000 'machine-checked proofs' declared by an integer, with proven=False everywhere (there are no clauses at all)
attacks.name: counter
attacks.rationale: the word 'machine-checked' lives only in the docstring; a counter incremented once per dead-end region enumerated by a reachability sweep -- not once per checked proof -- crosses 100 on any non-trivial grid, which is the ordinary way this field gets wired up.

attacks.claim: K10 = 4096 alongside 4096 clauses of kind 'theorem' every one of which has proven=False
attacks.name: dressed
attacks.rationale: K10 reads the integer and never looks at Clause.proven, which is the field that would encode 'machine-checked'; laying out 4096 unproven theorem clauses to match the counter is a deliberate dressing step, so this variant is not something a rig does by accident.

attacks.benign_window: K11 is a safe axis for K5/K6 only if revisions are counted per adjudicated manual change and every concept's admitted_revision indexes into that same sequence; used as a raw count it is a commit-frequency measurement.
attacks.claim: K11 = 1000 vs 1 for the same ten concepts; only the write granularity of the manual differs
attacks.name: bookkeeping
attacks.rationale: a harness that bumps the revision counter on every file write gets 1000, one that rewrites the manual once per episode gets 1; nothing about the theory changed, so the 'coarse axis' of the concept-birth timeline is a property of the writer, not of the learning.

attacks.benign_window: 0 revisions on a non-empty concept list should read as a broken writer, not as a stable manual; K11 cannot tell those apart.
attacks.claim: K11 = 100 vs 0 on two empty theories -- the metric never checks that anything was revised
attacks.name: empty
attacks.rationale: K11 has no thin() branch, so an arm that keeps a Theory object but never populates it still gets a numeric answer; a crashed or stubbed theory-writer therefore lands on the 0 end without any signal that the number is vacuous.

attacks.claim: K12 = 1.0 (6/6 beats closed) on a repair episode that spent zero environment actions; the evidence guard is satisfied by the string 'c0'
attacks.name: clause-tag
attacks.rationale: the guard asks for repair_actions OR env_actions OR changed_clause, and changed_clause is a free-text field a summariser fills in from the clause it *intended* to touch; any pipeline that records the target clause before doing the work passes the guard for free.

attacks.claim: K12 = 1.0 across 40 episodes, 240/240 beats, on a total budget of 40 environment actions (one per episode)
attacks.name: one-env-action
attacks.rationale: Repair.env_actions is a sum over beats, so a single action anywhere in the episode unlocks the whole six-beat claim; a harness that always takes one confirmatory step after editing the theory clears the guard on every episode without the beats meaning anything.

attacks.claim: K12 = 6.0 -- the episode declares its own denominator, so a 'share' exceeds 1
attacks.name: short-requirement
attacks.rationale: beats_required is per-episode and self-declared, and the metric divides by the sum of it without checking it against the six named beats; setting it to 1 is a deliberate act, so this is not an accident, but it shows K12's denominator is under the measured party's control.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 6 closed beats against a declared requirement of 1

attacks.claim: K12 = 1.0 where the entire evidence that a repair happened is the string ' '
attacks.name: whitespace
attacks.rationale: the guard is `not (r.repair_actions or r.env_actions or r.changed_clause)`, a truthiness test, so it separates 'unset' from 'set to anything at all' rather than 'no work' from 'work'; a space is not something a rig writes by accident, but it bounds how much the guard can possibly be asking for.

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: K13 = 0.0 from a Repair with no beats, no detection, no changed clause
attacks.name: empty-repair
attacks.rationale: repair_actions defaults to None, which falls through to env_actions, which sums an empty beat list to 0; any episode logged before its beats are written scores a perfect zero.

attacks.claim: K13 = 1e-06 by writing a large baseline_actions rather than a small repair
attacks.name: inflated-baseline
attacks.rationale: baseline_actions is a free integer never reconciled against len(run.steps); making the denominator large is the cheapest lever but it takes a deliberate choice of number.

attacks.claim: K13 = 0.0 averaged over one episode while a 500000-action repair sits in run.repairs, silently skipped
attacks.name: selective-annotation
attacks.rationale: `if not base or spent is None: continue` drops any episode missing a baseline, and the hardest repairs are exactly the ones whose pre-repair cost nobody managed to reconstruct.

attacks.claim: K13 = 0.0 with all six beats closed and every one of them costing 0 environment actions
attacks.name: zero-declared
attacks.rationale: A repair carried out purely by editing the manual -- no re-probing of the world -- genuinely costs zero environment actions, which is exactly the unverified repair the ratio should have penalised.

attacks.claim: K14 = 4096 bits over a manual of 512 concepts, 511 of which carry no compression account at all (support reports concepts=1)
attacks.name: censor
attacks.rationale: K14 filters to concepts whose compression_bits is not None, so the worst-case statistic is taken over the self-selected subset the estimator succeeded on; an estimator that gives up on exactly the concepts that compress badly produces this shape as its normal output.

attacks.claim: K14 = 1024 bits with all 256 concepts annotated -- a constant written into every concept passes the worst-case test
attacks.name: floor
attacks.rationale: a constant per-concept credit is what a stubbed or table-driven estimator emits, but writing 1024 into 256 records is a choice; it matters because K14 is a min and a min over a constant is maximally robust to the very outlier-hunting the metric exists for.

attacks.claim: K14 = 1000000 bits from a manual containing exactly one concept
attacks.name: single
attacks.rationale: a minimum over one element is that element, and the natural unit bug -- reporting the total encoded size of the corpus rather than the delta the concept bought -- is off by orders of magnitude in the favourable direction, so the 1000-bit threshold is cleared by a rounding convention rather than by compression.

attacks.claim: K2 = 1.0 with frame literally set to '3 adversarial gaps' -- the case the code's own thin() text says is incomparable
attacks.name: adversarial-three
attacks.rationale: The metric documents this exact failure in its refusal message and then returns ok anyway; choosing a three-pair held-out set and labelling it honestly is a choice an author makes, not a default.

attacks.claim: K2 = 1.0 on 1 held-out pair; the sampling-frame guard is satisfied by any truthy string
attacks.name: frame-string
attacks.rationale: held_out_frame is free text with no vocabulary and no comparison to the run, so any harness that fills the field at all -- even with a constant label -- clears the guard.

attacks.claim: K2 = 1.0 on 200 pairs the run itself both selected and graded
attacks.name: self-dealt
attacks.rationale: Held-out pairs and their grades come from the same writer as the manual, so a harness that generates negatives from the manual's own rules will agree with itself on every one of them.

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: K3 = 250 from 250 byte-identical clauses (same name, same kind)
attacks.name: duplicates
attacks.rationale: Append-only theory files plus a re-run loop duplicate clauses routinely; nothing in theorem_count() collapses by name.

attacks.claim: K3 = 120 from 120 Clause records whose only content is kind='invariant'
attacks.name: hundred
attacks.rationale: The count keys off a string field with no proof, evidence or uniqueness requirement, so any template that emits one clause per observed object type inflates it linearly in world size.

attacks.claim: K3 = 150 where every clause says proven=False, probe_pending=True, evidence_transitions=0
attacks.name: pending
attacks.rationale: The clause fields that would contradict the claim are all present in the model and all ignored by the metric; setting them to their most damning values on purpose is an attack, not an accident.

attacks.claim: K4 = 3.0 -- a 'share' of three, status ok
attacks.name: over-covered
attacks.rationale: Counting matched transitions across repeated visits to the same state while sizing the denominator by distinct states is an easy bookkeeping slip that pushes num past den.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: clause(s) o0, o1, o2, o3, o4, o5, o6, o7, o8, o9 claim more witnesses than the coverage denominator admits

attacks.claim: K4 = 1.0 computed over 1 clause while 200 clauses carry no coverage at all
attacks.name: single-annotated
attacks.rationale: The unannotated count is reported in support but never folded into the value, so any pipeline that annotates only the clauses it measured -- the normal case -- reports the mean of its easiest few.

attacks.claim: K4 = 1.0 from 60 clauses each covered by exactly 1 of 1 transitions
attacks.name: unit-fractions
attacks.rationale: A denominator floor is absent, and a clause mined from a single witnessed transition naturally has coverage 1/1, so a miner run on a short trace produces this shape by default.

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: K5 = 140 from 140 Concept records that carry a name and nothing else
attacks.name: alphabet
attacks.rationale: len(concepts) has no admission test beyond existence, so a segmenter that emits one concept per distinct sprite or colour crosses 100 on a mid-size grid without any of them being used.

attacks.claim: K5 = 110 where all 110 concepts have the identical name 'thing'
attacks.name: duplicates
attacks.rationale: The word table is a list, not a set; a revision loop that re-admits the same concept each pass grows it monotonically.

attacks.claim: K6 = 1000000.0 bits/concept from three integers nobody recomputed
attacks.name: inflated
attacks.rationale: compression_bits is taken on trust with no upper bound tied to the size of the trace it supposedly compresses, but writing 10^6 is a declaration, not a rounding error.

attacks.claim: K6 = 399808.0 bits/concept while 24 of the 25 concepts have negative gain
attacks.name: mean-hides
attacks.rationale: A mean over a heavy-tailed quantity is dominated by its largest term; one genuinely good abstraction plus a long tail of failed ones is the expected shape of real concept mining.

attacks.claim: K6 = 5000.0 'per admitted concept' over a denominator of 1 while K5 counts 100 admitted concepts
attacks.name: thin-denominator
attacks.rationale: The gains list silently drops concepts with compression_bits=None, so a pipeline that only bothers to cost the concepts it is proud of gets a mean over its own shortlist while K5 counts the whole table.

attacks.benign_window: K7 is only a sanity check on K6 if the same estimator, with a fixed sign convention, annotated every concept in the run; a K7 of 0 next to a K5 of 1000 should read as 'unaudited', not 'clean'.
attacks.claim: K7 = 1000 vs 0 on two manuals with the identical 1000 concepts; only the sign of a declared integer differs
attacks.name: sign
attacks.rationale: compression_bits is whatever the arm's own estimator wrote down; a sign convention (cost-of-encoding vs. bits-saved) flipped once in that estimator moves every concept across the boundary at the same time, which is exactly the 1000-vs-0 swing here.

attacks.benign_window: K7 is harmless only when read together with its own support field of_concepts and with K5: 0 of 1 accounted concepts is not the same reading as 0 of 400.
attacks.claim: K7 = 400 vs 0 on manuals of the same size; the low one simply declines to compute 399 of the 400 accounts
attacks.name: silence
attacks.rationale: an estimator that raises or times out on hard concepts and leaves compression_bits=None produces exactly the low run, so the arm with the *worst* compression tooling reports the cleanest diagnostic; that is an ordinary failure mode of an optional annotation, not sabotage.

attacks.claim: K8 = 1.0 at a million designed probes, with 50 clauses still flagged probe_pending and none proven
attacks.name: bulk
attacks.rationale: K8 never consults the clause table, so probe_pending clauses sitting unresolved next to a perfect executable rate raise no objection; declaring the two counters equal at any scale requires deliberately writing both, which is why this one is not accidental.

attacks.claim: K8 = 1.0 from a theory that designed exactly one probe and ran it
attacks.name: one-probe
attacks.rationale: the denominator is proposals, so the cheapest way to a perfect ratio is to propose almost nothing; any harness that only registers a probe design at the moment it dispatches it records designed==executable by construction and can never score below 1.0.

attacks.claim: K8 = 1000.0 -- a 'share' with no upper clamp; executable is allowed to exceed designed
attacks.name: overflow
attacks.rationale: a counter that increments once per probe *execution* while designs are counted per distinct template (retries, re-runs across levels) exceeds 1.0 without anybody intending it, and the metric prints the ratio anyway, so a share silently becomes an unbounded score.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: 1000 executable probes out of 1 designed

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: K9 = 100000 from a theory whose every other field is empty: no concepts, no clauses, no revisions
attacks.name: counter
attacks.rationale: playbook_entries is a self-reported integer with no object behind it, so a template that emits one 'prefer action a in state s' line per observed transition reaches six figures on a single long trace while containing no ordering, pruning or heuristic knowledge at all.

attacks.claim: K9 = 512 with 512 matching one-transition 'preference' clauses, so the count survives a cross-check against the clause table
attacks.name: transcription
attacks.rationale: each clause is a single memorised transition with coverage 1/1, which is what a rule miner emits when it fails to generalise; the playbook is then a transcript of the trace and K9 measures trace length, not policy.

attacks.claim: M1 = -1000.0; the metric accepts a delay that is physically impossible and ranks it best
attacks.name: precognition
attacks.rationale: No clamp at zero and no ordering assertion. Any pipeline that resolves first_seen from a level-entry event and first_used from an action log with different index origins (0-based vs 1-based, or per-level vs global) will emit negative delays silently.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: mechanism(s) recorded as first used before first seen (minimum delay -1000)

attacks.claim: M1 = 0.0 from a single hand-written annotation; the run has 3 steps and no mechanism use in them
attacks.name: same-step
attacks.rationale: The metric reads only run.truth.mechanisms and never cross-checks the step list, so the number is a property of the annotation file, not the run. An annotator who writes first_used=first_seen because that is the step where they noticed the mechanism produces this by convention, not by luck.

attacks.claim: M1 = 0.0 with a large n (used=60) so the support looks well-evidenced
attacks.name: saturate
attacks.rationale: Structurally different from same-step: it attacks the support field rather than the value. A reader who sanity-checks 'is this mean built on enough mechanisms?' sees used=60 and is reassured by fabricated breadth.

attacks.claim: M1 = 0.0 (perfect) on a run that used 1 of 100 mechanisms; M2 = 0.01 on the same run
attacks.name: survivorship
attacks.rationale: _delays() `continue`s past every mechanism with first_used None, so the mean is conditioned on success. An arm that learns one easy mechanism instantly and never grasps the other ninety-nine scores a perfect M1 with no intent to cheat; this is the normal shape of a weak run, not a contrived one.

defence.defence: a first-use or detection delay may not be negative; a mechanism used before it was visible is two counters with different origins, not a fast arm

attacks.claim: one 12-step run hits M1=0.0, M2=1.0, M4=0.0, M5=1.0, M6=1.0 simultaneously
attacks.name: all-family-sweep
attacks.rationale: The whole mechanism family is a function of two sidecar structures (Truth and the Repair list) that the arm supplies about itself; the 12 steps are decoration. There is no consistency check between the family's five live metrics, so one record satisfies all of them at once.

attacks.claim: M2 = 1.0 over 200 mechanisms that the run never observed becoming visible
attacks.name: never-seen
attacks.rationale: M2 tests only `first_used is not None`; it does not require first_seen, does not require the mechanism to appear in steps, and does not bound first_used by the run length. Structurally different from `single`: it inflates the numerator and denominator together rather than shrinking them.

attacks.claim: M2 = 1.0 from a one-element denominator
attacks.name: single
attacks.rationale: The denominator is len(mechanisms), which the run itself supplies. Any game whose annotator only bothered to write down the one mechanism the arm obviously used gets 1.0; sparse annotation and perfect uptake are the same number here.

attacks.claim: M2 = 1.0 on a run whose steps list is empty -- the arm never acted
attacks.name: zero-step-run
attacks.rationale: M2's `needs` are ('truth','mechanisms') only, so the metric never asks whether the run has steps. A harness that crashes after writing its truth sidecar but before flushing the trajectory produces exactly this record.

attacks.claim: M3 refuses on the other branch too: insufficient-data, value None
attacks.name: one-level
attacks.rationale: Both branches of the function terminate in thin(); confirms the stub rather than a data problem on my side.
attacks.reason: the run never reached a second level; transfer cannot be measured within one level

attacks.claim: M3 refuses: insufficient-data, value None, even with two levels and cross-level annotation
attacks.name: two-levels
attacks.rationale: Not an accident of my data -- the body has no ok() path at all. Reported as a failed attack.
attacks.reason: multi-level runs exist but the cross-level annotation schema is not yet defined; see STATUS.md

M3.note: attacked and not broken; see each attack's `reason` for the guard that refused it

attacks.claim: M4 = 0.0 while support says undetected_on_own_level=40 -- the manual noticed nothing, instantly
attacks.name: blind-but-instant
attacks.rationale: notes['earliest_detection'] outranks the detected flag (it is read first and detected is only a fallback), so a post-hoc 'when could it in principle have known?' annotation overwrites the actual detection record. The contradiction survives into the support dict, which is the tell.

attacks.claim: M4 = 0.0 from one self-reported detection_actions=0
attacks.name: instant
attacks.rationale: detection_actions is a self-report by the arm being scored, and 0 is the natural value when a harness initialises the counter and the detection is recognised on the same tick it is logged, i.e. an off-by-one in the instrumentation, not a lie.

attacks.claim: M4 = -500.0; no lower bound, so 'better than instantaneous' is expressible
attacks.name: negative
attacks.rationale: The delay is a difference of two action indices somewhere upstream; if the change-injection index and the detection index come from different counters (pre-injection baseline vs post-injection episode), the subtraction goes negative on its own.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: detection recorded before the change was injected (minimum -500 actions)

defence.defence: a first-use or detection delay may not be negative; a mechanism used before it was visible is two counters with different origins, not a fast arm

attacks.claim: M5 = 1.0 over 500 episodes with zero beats, zero detection_actions and zero theorems
attacks.name: bulk
attacks.rationale: Structurally different from one-detected: it defeats the obvious patch 'require a decent sample size'. Every other field on the Repair record is empty and the metric still returns a perfect score with episodes=500.

attacks.claim: M5 = 1.0 from a single boolean the scored arm sets itself
attacks.name: one-detected
attacks.rationale: detected is an unverified flag; nothing in the metric compares it against beats, clauses or steps. A harness whose default for `detected` is True (or which sets it when it writes the episode at all) yields 1.0 for every arm.

attacks.benign_window: Harmless only as a strict-zero check: M6 == 0.0 across episodes tells you no repair touched anything downstream. Any non-zero magnitude is uninterpretable without knowing what the reporter counted as a theorem.
attacks.claim: M6 = 1.0 vs 0.05 -- a factor of 20 -- from two runs identical except for two integers
attacks.name: dial
attacks.rationale: Both numerator and denominator are declared by the arm and are never reconciled with theory.clauses or theory.deadlock_theorems. How many theorems a manual 'had before' depends entirely on whether the implementation counts clauses, proven clauses, or derived corollaries -- a naming choice moves this diagnostic by an order of magnitude.

attacks.benign_window: A reader using M6 to sanity-check another metric should first assert 0 <= value <= 1; the code never does.
attacks.claim: M6 = 1000.0 vs 0.0 -- a 'share' with unit `share` that exceeds 1 by three orders of magnitude
attacks.name: unbounded
attacks.rationale: Structurally different from `dial`: it breaks the unit rather than the magnitude. There is no min(1.0, ...) and no assertion that invalidated_theorems <= theorems_before, so the declared unit `share` is not enforced anywhere.
attacks.reason: incoherent record: episode(s) ep01 invalidate more theorems than the manual held

defence.defence: a value declared unit="share" may not exceed one, and a numerator may not exceed its denominator; such a record is refused as incoherent rather than reported as excellent

attacks.claim: P1 = 60.0 even though every model call is marked is_error=True
attacks.name: failure-free-by-omission
attacks.rationale: P1 counts len(run.calls), not successful calls, and counts steps the logger chose to write; a harness that drops rejected actions before logging turns a broken run into a high score by omission alone.

attacks.claim: P1 = 100.0 while every action is the identical no-op leaving state unchanged
attacks.name: noop-saturation
attacks.rationale: A polling/keep-alive loop or a stuck controller that re-issues the same action until a timeout logs hundreds of non-failing steps against a handful of prompts; nothing in P1 asks whether the state moved.

attacks.claim: P1 = 5000.0 from a single model call that emits one batched macro
attacks.name: one-call-batch
attacks.rationale: Any harness that lets the model emit a list of actions per turn, or that replays a recorded macro after one prompt, produces exactly this shape without anyone trying to game it.

attacks.claim: P2 = 200.0 because the half-way boundary is read off a self-reported step_idx
attacks.name: boundary-lie
attacks.rationale: Harnesses commonly stamp step_idx as 'the step this call was made before', so every planning call in a plan-then-execute agent legitimately carries step_idx=0; that alone puts the whole run in the second half.

attacks.claim: P2 = 100.0 from four honestly-tied calls, all of them made in the first four steps
attacks.name: late-success
attacks.rationale: If the model is only consulted while it is failing and the harness then runs an unattended scripted tail, every successful step lands after the boundary; no lie about step_idx is needed, only that calls stop early.

attacks.claim: P2 stays near zero on the proportional branch no matter how many steps are laid out
attacks.name: proportional-floor
attacks.rationale: This is a deliberate probe of the fallback branch rather than a score attack; the proportional split defines first/second from the same constant rate, so only integer-floor slack (bounded well under 1) leaks.

attacks.claim: P3 = 0.0 while the agent repeats one no-op action 500 times
attacks.name: counter-keys
attacks.rationale: State keys are routinely hashed from a frame that embeds a step counter, score, or timestamp; any such key makes every state unique and P3 identically zero for free.

attacks.claim: P3 = 0.0 from a four-step run that dies immediately, on a single window
attacks.name: sparse-observations
attacks.rationale: A run that crashes after three steps clears the len(keys) >= 3 gate with exactly one window and reports the best possible backtrack rate; early termination is the single most common way real runs end.

attacks.claim: P3 = 0.0 on a run that cycles A->B->C->A forever and makes no progress
attacks.name: three-cycle
attacks.rationale: The window compares keys[i+1] with keys[i-1], so it only detects period-2 oscillation; a stuck agent whose loop has any other period scores a perfect zero, and three-move loops are common in grid worlds.

attacks.claim: P4 = 0.05 after 10000 failed actions, against an honest optimal of 20
attacks.name: failed-steps-are-free
attacks.rationale: P4 divides len(run.ok_steps) by optimal, so any action the environment rejects is free; a brute-force agent whose illegal moves bounce off the rules looks more efficient than optimal without deceiving anyone.

attacks.claim: P4 = 0.001 because the denominator is read from the run's own Truth record
attacks.name: inflated-optimal
attacks.rationale: No harness accidentally writes optimal_steps=1000 for a one-step win; this is a pure trust attack showing P4's 'ground truth' is run-supplied and unverified by the metric.

attacks.claim: P4 = 0.0 -- a perfect-and-then-some score from zero successful actions
attacks.name: won-but-failed
attacks.rationale: won and failed are independent flags on Step, and a terminal transition that both wins and errors (win detected on a call the harness marks failed, e.g. a timeout on the final ACK) empties ok_steps entirely.

attacks.benign_window: Harmless only if P5 is read alongside a fixed, documented definition of 'failed' from the same adapter; across adapters it ranks nothing.
attacks.claim: P5 = 1.0 vs 0.005 on runs with identical actions and identical state keys
attacks.name: flag-only
attacks.rationale: The two runs differ only in a boolean the logger sets; harnesses disagree on whether a rejected action is a failed step or simply not a step, so the same behaviour lands anywhere on this axis depending on the adapter.

attacks.claim: X1 = 0.0 while the board hash is literally constant across all 300 steps
attacks.name: counter-in-key
attacks.rationale: Harnesses routinely build a state key by serialising the whole observation record, and observation records routinely carry a step index, frame counter or timestamp. One such field makes every state unique and drives X1 to 0 with no exploration whatsoever.

attacks.claim: X1 = 0.0 from a two-step run that crashed before doing anything
attacks.name: early-exit
attacks.rationale: A run that dies after two steps clears the len(seen) < 2 guard by exactly one step and then scores perfectly; crash-early runs are the most common junk record in any batch harness.

attacks.claim: X1 = 0.0 over 300 steps that press one button and relabel the screen each time
attacks.name: fresh-labels
attacks.rationale: Minting a brand-new label every step is a deliberate choice here, but it costs nothing: the metric consumes the arm's own naming of state and has no way to notice 300 identical presses.

attacks.claim: X2 = 1.0 on a 300-step run of which 297 steps were rejected spam
attacks.name: failed-curtain
attacks.rationale: _transition_keys drops failed steps entirely, so a run that spent 99% of its budget being refused is scored only on the three steps that landed -- an arm that mostly fails looks maximally exploratory.

attacks.claim: X2 = 1.0 from a single frozen state and 300 never-repeated action names
attacks.name: fresh-actions
attacks.rationale: Agents that emit parameterised actions (click at x,y; type <string>) almost never repeat an action string verbatim, so the transition set is novel by construction even when the world does not move.

attacks.claim: X2 = 1.0 on 300 repetitions of a single action
attacks.name: fresh-states
attacks.rationale: The key is prev_state|action and only one of the two halves has to vary. Any harness whose state key is even slightly noisy -- a frame counter, an animation phase, an RNG seed echoed in the observation -- gets X2 = 1.0 while pressing the same button forever.

attacks.claim: X3 = 1.0 for a run that dies in an infinite loop over its whole second half
attacks.name: explore-then-jam
attacks.rationale: Explore-then-get-stuck is the single most common real trajectory shape, and X3 pays it the maximum score: the metric rewards the last quarter being *empty* of novelty, which is exactly what being stuck looks like. This is an inversion, not just a fill.

attacks.claim: X3 = 1.0 from eight steps, the smallest run the guard admits
attacks.name: minimum-length
attacks.rationale: quarter = len(keys)//4 = 2 here, so the whole statistic rests on four transitions; short truncated runs land on the extreme values of X3 constantly and there is no sample-size floor beyond eight.

attacks.claim: X4 = 0.04 for a run that ends in a real 50-step dead stall
attacks.name: dilute-the-stall
attacks.rationale: The streak is normalised by run length, so cheap high-volume stepping buys immunity: a harness that batches many micro-actions per decision inflates the denominator without inflating the stall.

attacks.claim: X4 = 0.0 on 300 identical presses relabelled as 300 states
attacks.name: no-streak
attacks.rationale: Same mechanism as X1: X4 reads the arm's own state labels, so any monotone field in the observation record (tick, frame, score, elapsed ms) makes the no-progress streak structurally unreachable.

attacks.claim: X4 = 0.003... while the arm bounces between one hub and one-shot side states
attacks.name: sawtooth
attacks.rationale: `current = 0` resets on *any* new label, so a single novel state between repeats truncates the streak. Agents that return to a menu or home screen between probes produce exactly this sawtooth.

attacks.benign_window: X5 is harmless only as a floor check -- 'this run saw more than a handful of distinct states' -- and only when state_key is a hash of a canonicalised environment frame produced by the harness, never by the arm.
attacks.claim: X5 = 500 vs 1 from two runs that take the identical 500 actions
attacks.name: label-dial
attacks.rationale: The two runs differ only in the naming convention of state_key, not in behaviour; whether a harness hashes the raw frame or a canonicalised one swings this diagnostic by 500x with no change to the agent.

attacks.claim: one poverty-certified run clears the X1/X2/X4/X6 thresholds simultaneously
attacks.name: family-sweep
attacks.rationale: Deliberately constructed, but it shows the family shares a single point of failure rather than four: all of X1, X2, X4 and X6 read only arm-supplied strings, so one relabelling convention satisfies all of them at once and the four metrics are not independent evidence.

attacks.claim: X6 = 1.0 on 200 consecutive failures with a fresh action name each time
attacks.name: round-robin
attacks.rationale: A scripted sweep over an action list -- the standard fallback when an agent has no idea what to do -- changes action after every refusal by construction, so the least adaptive possible policy maxes the metric.

attacks.claim: X6 = 1.0 decided by exactly one of 400 steps
attacks.name: single-window
attacks.rationale: The `windows == 0` guard is the only sample floor, so one lucky failure early in a long run fixes the metric at 1.0; near-flawless runs with a single stumble are common and will be scored on that stumble alone.

attacks.claim: X6 = 1.0 from a two-symbol ABAB oscillation that ignores every refusal
attacks.name: two-stroke
attacks.rationale: X6 only compares consecutive action strings for inequality; a period-2 loop satisfies that on every window while demonstrably learning nothing, since it re-issues the refused action two steps later.

verdict.rule: S1 metric answered AND S2 reached the pre-registered target AND S3 poverty certificate passed -> gameable. gameable AND accidental AND NOT defended -> reference. R1: V9 never promotes on silence. R2: a defence that would promote needs more attack variants than tests.
